finding: The exit-0 rule buys its correctness by spending the most expensive round-trip tp has on a unit that has no work. §4.2's own skip table marks `no-checklist-items` and `no-spec-change` as 'Drops a unit? no / Drops a prompt? yes', so under `tp run` the driver spawns a full runner process (one per unit, spec/0.35.0.md §3.3.1) for a role that will receive `prompts: []`. That agent pays its entire startup context to discover it has nothing to judge, produces no rows, and leaves nothing for `promoteRoleFindings` to promote. §4.2 asks only 'should the brief exit 0 or 2' and never asks the cheaper question — should the process exist at all. Both skip reasons are computable before spawning (the checklist derives from the spec text; `no-spec-change` derives from `--diff-from`), which is why emission already computes them.
suggestion: Apply the two prompt-only skips in `engine.roleUnits` as well, so no unit is created for a role that will emit no prompt, and say so in §4.2 as the primary fix. Keep exit 0 for the interactive/typo case, where no process was spawned and the cost is one invocation — then the exit-0 rule is a courtesy rather than the mechanism that makes a wasted agent legal.

finding: The exit-2 condition is a conjunction: a name exits 2 only when it is 'absent from the corpus for either phase, from skipped_roles, and from the built-ins'. An auditor role name passed to tp review is present in the corpus for the audit phase, so it fails that condition and is routed into the exit-0 branch — which requires 'the role's own entry present in skipped_roles, carrying the reason tp already computes'. No such entry exists. Measured: tp review spec/0.36.0.md reports skipped_roles as the empty array while tp audit spec/0.36.0.md emits spec-coverage, so tp review --role spec-coverage has no computed reason to echo and no entry to present. The spec's own routing rule sends a case into a branch whose required response is undefined for it, and §6.3 covers neither side — test 8's subject is a name recognised nowhere, test 9's is the five skip reasons.
suggestion: Rule the cross-phase case explicitly, in one of two ways. Either narrow the exit-2 condition to 'absent from the corpus for THIS phase', so tp review --role spec-coverage exits 2 with the hint listing what the invocation would have emitted — which is what an operator who typed an auditor name into a review command actually needs. Or keep exit 0 and define the skipped_roles entry tp must synthesise, naming the reason slug (for example other-phase) so the echoed reason is testable. Add the chosen case to §6.3 as its own numbered test.

finding: §4.2's new exit-0 rule creates a unit state that the shipped v0.35.0 Stop fence refuses, and this spec says it does not change that fence. §4.2 rules that a corpus role skipped `no-checklist-items` or `no-spec-change` is still spawned as a unit, that its own brief exits 0 with `prompts: []`, and that this 'lets that unit finish cleanly and record nothing, which is the correct outcome for a role that had nothing to review'. But a unit whose invocation emits no prompt receives no `output_path`, and therefore receives neither §2.2's nor §3.2's clause and no statement of where to write. Verified in the shipped hook `hooks/stop-role-incomplete.sh` (lines 263-294, the `spec/0.35.0.md` §6.2 Stop hook that §3.3 cites as unchanged): the stop is refused with exit 2 and the reason `it does not exist: $TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson.part` unless that file is present. So 'record nothing' is exactly the outcome the fence blocks, and the driver's promote step has nothing to rename. §4.2 changes the brief without saying what an empty-prompt unit owes the round.
suggestion: State in §4.2 that a unit whose `--role` invocation emits `prompts: []` must still create an empty findings file at `$TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson.part` (the hook's own remedy text already says an empty file passes), and add a §6.4 test that runs the `no-checklist-items` unit's brief and then asserts the Stop predicate holds. Alternatively state that the empty-prompt case is an escalation rather than a clean finish -- but pick one, because today §4.2 and `spec/0.35.0.md` §6.2 disagree about the same unit.

finding: §4.2's newly written exit-0 branch is unbuildable for the names its own exit-2 definition admits. Exit 2 is reserved for "a name tp recognises nowhere — absent from the corpus for either phase, from skipped_roles, and from the built-ins". By that definition `tp review --role go-safety` (an AUDIT corpus role, so recognised via "the corpus for either phase") is not an exit-2 case and must take the exit-0 branch, which requires "the role's own entry present in skipped_roles, carrying the reason tp already computes". No such entry exists: internal/engine/skipped.go's five reasons are all computed over the roles of THIS phase, so review's skipped_roles never mentions an auditor. The implementer must either invent a sixth reason the spec never names, or emit an entry with an empty reason, or violate one of the two rules. The same hole swallows `--role test-planner` in default mode: §4.2 itself notes test-planner is "in neither" corpus, names only `regression` as a reserved built-in, and so leaves undecided whether test-planner is a built-in (exit 0, no reason available) or recognised nowhere (exit 2) — and §6.3 test 9 exercises only the five in-phase reasons, so neither case is tested.
suggestion: Define the recognition set as exactly {roles the current PHASE's corpus contains} ∪ {roles present in this invocation's skipped_roles} ∪ {the reserved built-ins, enumerated by name}, so an other-phase role name and `test-planner` in default mode both fall to exit 2 with the existing single hint. If cross-phase names must instead exit 0, state the literal reason string tp is to synthesise (e.g. `wrong-phase`), add it to internal/engine/skipped.go's vocabulary, and add a §6.3 test for it.

finding: §4.2's two-branch rule is a trichotomy presented as a dichotomy, and the third case is one §4.2 itself names. The exit-0 branch requires 'the role's own entry present in `skipped_roles`, carrying the reason tp already computes'; the exit-2 branch is reserved for 'a name tp recognises nowhere -- absent from the corpus for either phase, from `skipped_roles`, and from the built-ins'. `skipped_roles` only ever carries corpus roles plus `regression`: `internal/engine/skipped.go` defines exactly five reasons (`no-checklist-items`, `no-spec-change`, `domain-mismatch`, `no-baseline`, `disabled-by-spec`) and appends only corpus ids. So `test-planner` -- which §4.2 bullet 2 names as a role tp emits under `--perspective testing` and which is 'in neither' the corpus nor the active set -- and `verifier`, which §4.2.1 names as `--verify`'s role, satisfy neither branch in default mode: they are recognised (so not exit 2) and they have no `skipped_roles` entry to echo (so the exit-0 branch's own guarantee is unmeetable). Confirmed on this round's emission: `skipped_roles` is `[]` while five roles are emitted.
suggestion: Add the third rule explicitly: a name tp recognises in some other mode but that this invocation neither emits nor skips exits 0 with `prompts: []` and an empty `skipped_roles` (or exits 2 with a hint naming the mode that would emit it). Whichever is chosen, drop the promise that the exit-0 case always carries a `skipped_roles` entry, and extend §6.3 test 9 -- which today sweeps only the five reasons -- with a `--role test-planner` and a `--role verifier` case in default mode.

finding: §4.3's P2 claim prices the split script and nothing else ('more invocations, but no script to write, skip or mis-write'), and on the human path the measurement inverts the release's own headline. An invocation is not free: `internal/cli/review.go:540-543` runs every registered `workflow.checks` entry on each emitting `tp review`, and §2.2 records that the same command rewrites `spec/.tp-review/<base>/snapshot-round-N.md`. Measured on this spec's round 5, current binary: the unrestricted payload is 182,926 B, of which 173,514 B are prompts and 3,740 B are the non-prompt keys (`structured_elements` 2,549, `review_loop` 1,059, spec/spec_path 126, `skipped_roles` 2). Five per-role invocations emit the same 173,514 prompt bytes plus 5 x 3,740 = 18,700 B of repeated keys — 192,214 B, +9,288 B (+5.1%) into the orchestrator's own context — and run the mechanical checks five times and rewrite the snapshot five times. The orchestrator only avoids the byte increase by redirecting each invocation to a file, which is a script, the artifact §4.3 claims `--role` removes.
suggestion: State the N-invocation price in §4.3 next to the 90.6%: N x (non-prompt keys + one `workflow.checks` execution + one snapshot rewrite), with this round's figures. Then say plainly that the win is the `tp run` path (where the N invocations already happened) and that on the human path `--role` trades ~5% more total bytes and N check runs for the deleted split script — which may still be the right trade, but it is a trade, not a reduction.

finding: §6.1's whole construction rests on a seam that does not exist and that the spec does not ask for: "the test calls the prompt builder twice, once with the append enabled and once without". `buildReviewPrompts` has no such toggle, and §6.1 never says which of the three ways to create one is meant, each of which an implementer must weigh against this repo's own gate: (a) add a bool parameter to the production builder — `unparam` flags a parameter that production always passes the same value for, and it is dead production surface `deadcode`/`unused` will notice; (b) add a package-level var the test flips — not race-safe under `go test -race ./...`, which is step 1 of the project gate; (c) factor the append into its own exported/unexported function and have the test call the builder and then RE-DERIVE the baseline by stripping the suffix — which makes test 5 tautological, because it would then assert 467 == len(the 467 bytes it just removed) and would pass on any clause text whatsoever, defeating the sentence "rewording either clause, or dropping the strip, fails it". The choice is observable in whether test 5 can fail, so it is not an implementation detail.
suggestion: Name the seam. State that the append is a separate function, e.g. `appendUnitClauses(body string) string`, that the builder calls last, and that the tests assert `appendUnitClauses(b) == want` and `len(appendUnitClauses(b)) - len(b) == 467` over a body captured from the builder BEFORE the call — or specify a builder option struct with an explicit `SkipUnitClauses` field and say it is test-only and how it survives the deadcode/unparam steps of the project gate.

finding: Test 3 claims its suffix comparison 'pins order, position and every separator byte in one assertion'. It cannot pin the one byte §2.3 calls 'not optional and not cosmetic'. If an implementation appends without stripping the body's pre-existing trailing newline, the emitted body ends with that old LF followed by LF LF + clause 2.2 + LF LF + clause 3.2 — and the asserted suffix (LF LF + clause 2.2 + LF LF + clause 3.2) still matches, because a suffix match cannot see the byte in front of it. Test 3 therefore passes on precisely the construction §1's -1 row exists to forbid. Only test 5's exact integer catches it, so §6.2's strongest-sounding assertion is silent on the release's most likely off-by-one, and an implementer who reads test 3's claim has no reason to expect test 5 to be the discriminating one.
suggestion: Make test 3 an equality rather than a suffix match: assert the whole emitted body equals the pre-clause body with its trailing newline removed, plus the suffix — which is what §7 criterion 3 already states. If the suffix form is kept for cheapness, add the missing clause explicitly: 'and the byte immediately preceding the suffix is not LF'. Either way, drop 'every separator byte' from test 3's claim, since the separator that matters most is the one it does not see.

finding: Tests 13 and 14 are explicitly two-phase — test 13 names 'the audit-role equivalent', test 14 runs 'for each unit BuildNextUnits returns' — but test 15 states an unscoped set equality: 'the emitted role set minus the unit set equals exactly {regression}'. Measured on the freshly built binary against this repository's corpus, tp audit spec/0.36.0.md emits ax-contract, go-safety, maintainability-conventions and spec-coverage, with no regression entry, while tp review spec/0.36.0.md emits regression as a fifth prompt. For the audit phase the difference set is empty, so test 15 as written fails there. The guard clause 'on a round where regression is emitted' can be read three ways — audit is out of scope, audit is a vacuous pass, or audit must satisfy the same equality — and two engineers write three different tests. §4.4 leans on test 15 ('§6.4 test 15 pins that visibility to an exact set') for a claim that has no audit-side referent at all.
suggestion: Scope test 15 to tp review explicitly, and give the audit phase its own clause so the asymmetry §4.1 measures is asserted rather than inferred: 'for tp audit the emitted role set equals the unit set exactly, since no built-in role is auto-appended.' That also makes a future audit-side built-in fail a test deliberately, which is the property test 15 was written to have.

finding: Gate criterion 3 and §6.3 test 12 both call the appended text a '467-byte suffix'. Measured from §2.2's and §3.2's verbatim strings, the suffix is 2 + 287 + 2 + 177 = 468 bytes; 467 is the NET delta, and only because §2.3 also strips one pre-existing trailing newline — which is exactly what §1's table shows with its -1 row. Criterion 3's construction, 'the v0.36.0 body equals the pre-clause body with its trailing newline removed plus §2.3's 467-byte suffix', therefore describes a body one byte shorter than the real emission, and a test written literally from it can never pass. Test 12's 'differs from the same tree's pre-clause emission only by the 467-byte suffix inside each prompts[].prompt' repeats the same conflation. §1 fixed the 468-vs-467 confusion for the net figure and it has reappeared attached to the suffix.
suggestion: Call the appended text the 468-byte suffix everywhere and reserve 467 for the net delta. Restate criterion 3 as: 'the v0.36.0 body equals the pre-clause body with its trailing newline removed, plus §2.3's 468-byte suffix — a net difference of 467 bytes, as §1 tabulates.' Restate test 12 as a net 467-byte difference rather than a 467-byte suffix. Test 5 already measures the net and stays as it is.

finding: Gate criterion 3 cannot be run by the mechanism §7 costs. Criterion 3 requires "the pre-clause body" for every spec in the repository, but §7's cost model consists only of `tp review`/`tp audit` invocations, and no shipped invocation emits a pre-clause body — §6.1 obtains that baseline by calling the prompt builder twice IN-PROCESS, which is a Go test, not a CLI. So criterion 3 is either (a) not runnable at all from the gate as priced, or (b) requires a new flag or build tag that exposes the un-appended emission, which would be new user-facing surface this release never specifies and Non-Goal 7 does not cover. This is the same shape §6.1 just diagnosed and fixed for the tests: §7 reintroduces the unobtainable baseline at the binary level while §6.1's fix lives only at the package level.
suggestion: Either scope criterion 3 to the package-level tests (say that §6.2 tests 3 and 5 ARE criterion 3, run over a corpus of specs via a table-driven Go test that calls the builder, not the CLI), or name the seam that lets the binary emit the pre-clause body and specify its flag, exit codes and whether it ships. Do not leave a release-blocking criterion whose only stated implementation is an invocation that cannot produce one of its two operands.

finding: The release gate is specified as a read-only measurement and is not one, by this spec's own evidence. §7 prices it as 'roughly 150 emissions, seconds of CPU, no network and no agent. It is a test, not a cycle.' But §2.2 of this same document establishes that `tp review <spec>` 'writes repository state as a side effect -- it takes the round's snapshot under `spec/.tp-review/<base>/`', and cites two observations of exactly that. Verified again while reviewing: the emission that produced this round's prompt rewrote `spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/snapshot-round-5.md` (mtime 14:26:24, two minutes before this finding). So a gate that runs `tp review` and `tp audit` once per spec plus once per emitted role refreshes -- and for a never-reviewed spec creates -- the same `spec/.tp-review/` tree whose snapshot drift (§7's own '35 of 145, 24%') is the evidence §7 rests its first paragraph on. §6.1 fixes exactly this hazard for the unit tests ('the test's own temporary state directory'); §7 gets no equivalent.
suggestion: Give §7 the isolation §6.1 already gives §6: run the gate against a copy of the tree, or with the review state directory redirected, and say so in the section rather than leaving the side effect to be discovered. Then re-price it -- the current cost line accounts for CPU but not for the state every invocation writes.

finding: The release gate's only mechanism writes the repository state the gate is measuring, and §7 prices it as if it were read-only. §7 specifies "One `tp review` and one `tp audit` per spec, plus one per emitted role" and calls the cost "seconds of CPU, no network and no agent". But this same spec, in §2.2, records the measured counter-evidence: "the orchestrator, whose read-only measurement invocation rewrote `snapshot-round-3.md`" — `tp review <spec>` takes the round's snapshot under `spec/.tp-review/<base>/` as a side effect. Running the gate over every spec with review history therefore rewrites 15 specs' snapshots (and, for released specs whose text has moved on, replaces the snapshot each recorded round was reviewed against — the exact drift §7's own paragraph measures at 35/145). An implementer has no stated way to run the gate without that write: §7 names no `--no-state`-style seam, and §6.1 rejects `--no-state` implicitly by requiring a round where `regression` is emitted, which round 1 is not.
suggestion: State the gate's isolation explicitly: run every emission against a scratch copy of the repository (rsync/`git worktree`) or against a `TP_*`-pinned temporary state directory, and assert `git status --porcelain spec/.tp-review/` is empty after the gate. If a snapshot write is accepted, say so and say that the gate must run before the release commit, not after.

finding: §7 opens by naming the hazard this release must be gated against — 'every mechanism in this release hides, regroups or narrows what a reviewer sees', the v0.34.0 §7.1 shape — and criterion 2 claims to be 'the assertion that actually catches suppression: a role that stops being emitted, or an entry that changes when selected alone, fails it'. Only the second half is true. All three criteria compare --role output against the unrestricted output of the same tree, and the role list under test is enumerated from that same unrestricted payload ('for each role the unrestricted invocation emits', 'the union of the per-role invocations'). If the unrestricted emission itself drops a role, every criterion still passes: criterion 1 compares only the roles that remain, criterion 2's union equals the now-smaller unrestricted payload, criterion 3 compares bodies pairwise. The gate verifies that --role is faithful to emission; nothing in it verifies that emission is faithful to the panel, which is the failure v0.34.0 §7.1 actually produced.
suggestion: Add a criterion with a referent external to the emission under test: for each phase, the emitted role set equals the active corpus for that phase plus exactly the built-ins the round's own conditions admit (regression for review from round 2 when the spec changed or findings resolved fixed; none for audit), asserted as set equality. If that is judged out of size, restate criterion 2's purpose honestly as 'catches suppression introduced by --role', which is what it measures, so the gate does not read as covering a hazard it leaves open.

finding: §7's scope predicate and its cost basis select two different sets, and the escape clause it adds for safety is empty in this repository. The gate runs 'per spec that has a role corpus' and is priced on 'this repository's 15 specs'. The corpus is repo-level, not per-spec: `.tp/reviewers/` holds four files and `.tp/auditors/` four, resolved for every spec (per-spec activation only *deactivates* roles). So the predicate 'has a role corpus' selects all 39 files in `spec/`, while 15 is the count of directories under `spec/.tp-review/` -- the specs that have already been reviewed, which is a different property entirely. The cost is therefore understated by roughly 2.5x, and the closing sentence 'A spec with no role corpus is named as out of scope rather than silently skipped' names a set that is empty here, so it can never fire and never be tested.
suggestion: Say which set the gate runs over and derive both the scope and the cost from it. If the intent is 'specs with recorded review state', say that -- it is the property 15 measures, and it is also the only set for which running the gate does not create new state (see the §7 side-effect finding). If the intent really is every spec, restate the cost against 39 and say what the gate does with the 24 specs that have no tasks file.

finding: 467 is a derived number that the spec hard-codes in five places (§1 prose, §1's table row, §6.2 test 5, §6.3 test 12, §7 criterion 3) and then asks a test to assert as an exact integer. No agent, driver or operator branches on 467; its only stated function is 'so rewording either clause, or dropping the strip, fails it' — which test 3 already delivers, since a suffix comparison against the two clause strings plus their separators fails on any reword, any separator change and any missing strip, byte for byte. So test 5 adds a second assertion over the same bytes and five sites that must be edited in lockstep the first time either clause is touched; the round-4 draft's 468 is the failure mode already demonstrated once.
suggestion: Derive it: have test 5 assert the delta equals len(clauseA) + len(clauseB) + 4 - 1 computed from the same two constants the code emits, and have §1 present 467 as the value of that expression on today's strings rather than as a contract. Then a reword updates one place and both tests still fail on a dropped strip.

finding: §2.3 claims test 3 pins something test 3 cannot see, and §6.2 repeats the claim. §2.3's construction is load-bearing on the strip ('The -1 is not optional and not cosmetic', §1), and §6.2 test 3 is described as asserting the suffix 'which pins order, position and every separator byte in one assertion'. It does not pin the strip. If the pre-existing body ends in LF (which §1 states it always does) and an implementation appends without stripping, the body ends `...x LF LF LF <clause2> LF LF <clause3>` -- and the required suffix `LF LF <clause2> LF LF <clause3>` still matches, because a suffix comparison cannot see the extra LF that precedes it. The strip is caught only by test 5's exact 467, which §6.2 does say ('or dropping the strip, fails it'), so the defect is the overstated claim in two places, not a hole in coverage.
suggestion: Drop 'every separator byte' from §2.3 and from test 3's description, and say instead that test 3 pins order and adjacency while test 5 pins the strip. Or make test 3 discriminating by asserting the body's last N bytes where N is the exact suffix length *and* that byte N+1 is not LF.

finding: The §4.2 rewrite deleted the only sentence that ruled on the rest of the payload and replaced it with nothing, so the emitted JSON under `--role` is undefined outside `prompts[]`. Round 4's §4.1 carried "Every other top-level key is unchanged"; §4.2 now specifies only that `prompts[]` is "reduced to the single entry whose `role` equals `<name>`", plus one incidental constraint (the exit-0 branch requires `skipped_roles` to still carry the named role's entry). An implementer must guess on every other key the payload actually emits: `review_loop.instruction`, which today reads "For each prompt, spawn a sub-agent via the Agent tool. Merge findings..." and is panel-shaped instruction text that a single-role caller is not meant to act on; `skipped_roles` in the exit-0-with-one-prompt case; `structured_elements`; and the `spec`/`spec_path` group. This is not the question of whether the instruction TEXT is true — it is that no rule at all now governs the keys, and §6.3 test 6 asserts only on `prompts[]`, so both a filtering and a non-filtering implementation pass every test in §6.
suggestion: Restore an explicit rule in §4.2 — e.g. "every top-level key other than `prompts[]` is emitted exactly as the unrestricted invocation emits it, `skipped_roles` included" — and, if `review_loop.instruction` must change for a single-role caller, specify its `--role` wording and add a §6.3 assertion for it. Whichever way it goes, add one test that compares the `--role` payload to the unrestricted payload with `prompts[]` removed.

finding: §4.2's central definition is circular. 'The match set is the set this same invocation would emit' -- but the invocation being defined *carries* `--role`, so what it emits is precisely what the match set decides. Read literally the definition is satisfied by any behaviour, including emitting nothing. The section's own worked examples show the intended reading is the unrestricted invocation (`regression` 'is emitted and is in no corpus', `--perspective testing` 'emits `test-planner`'), and §7 criterion 2 depends on that reading -- it unions the per-role invocations and compares against 'the unrestricted `prompts[]`'. But §4.2 never says 'unrestricted', and this is the one sentence three tests (6, 7, 9) and two gate criteria are derived from.
suggestion: Reword to 'the set the same invocation *without* `--role` would emit' -- same intent, no self-reference, and it matches the phrasing §7 criterion 2 already uses.

finding: §4.2's last bullet states two normative rules and §6.3 tests neither. First, '--role takes exactly one value. It is a string flag, not repeatable' — but a plain string flag accepts a repeated occurrence and silently keeps the last, so as prescribed the rule has no observable failure and no test can distinguish an implementation that honours it from one that does not; the spec would have to ask for an explicit refusal for 'not repeatable' to mean anything a test can see. Second, an empty --role value 'is refused as an unknown role rather than treated as absent, so flag given empty and flag absent are never the same command' — this is the case an operator actually hits when a shell variable expands to nothing, and it is the difference between exit 2 and a full panel, yet test 8's subject is 'a name tp recognises nowhere', which does not obviously cover the empty string.
suggestion: Add both to §6.3: 'an empty --role value exits 2 with the unknown-role hint, and is not treated as an absent flag' and, for arity, either 'a repeated --role exits 2 with a hint naming the repetition' — which makes the not-repeatable rule enforceable — or, if last-wins is the intended behaviour, say that instead of 'not repeatable' and assert it.

finding: §4.3's headline reduction compares a payload figure against a prompt-body figure, in a spec that elsewhere insists every figure name its denominator. §4.1's 'Payload' column is not the payload: 49,567 + 82,160 = 131,727 exactly, so the column is the sum of `prompts[].prompt` bodies. §4.3 then restates that number as what a unit *receives* ('a role unit receives 131,727 bytes to read 12,376 of them ... with the brief of §4.2.2 it receives only its own'). It does not receive only its own: `--role` is specified to reduce `prompts[]` and nothing else, so `structured_elements`, `skipped_roles`, `review_loop` and the JSON escaping of the retained prompt all survive. Measured on this spec's round 5, current binary: the whole emitted payload is 182,691 B against 173,467 B of decoded prompt bodies, and a payload reduced to the architect entry alone is 27,579 B against a 21,001-byte prompt -- 24% of what the unit actually receives is not its prompt. Like for like, the reduction is ~85%, not the 90.6% §4.3 and §4.1 both assert.
suggestion: Either relabel §4.1's column 'prompt bytes' and have §4.3 say 'prompt bytes handed to units' on both sides of the ratio, or measure the real payload on both sides and quote that figure. Also say explicitly whether `--role` leaves the other top-level keys intact -- §4.2 no longer states it either way since the round-4 'every other top-level key is unchanged' sentence was dropped.

finding: §6.1 makes four inputs load-bearing — the round number, the loop budget, the consecutive-clean count and the output_path — and pins them with one mechanism: they 'are fixed explicitly by the test's own temporary state directory, not by a comment saying they are'. The named mechanism does not reach one of the four. The loop budget the prompt prints ('Loop budget: review round N; K consecutive clean round(s) required, M so far') is the workflow convergence policy, which resolves under the documented precedence CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in and lives in .tp/config.json at the repository root; the review state directory holds recorded rounds and snapshots, not policy. A test that creates only a temp state dir therefore inherits this repository's policy and its emitted bytes change when .tp/config.json does — which is the exact failure mode §6.1 wrote this paragraph to prevent. For the 467-byte delta of test 5 both sides cancel, but tests 6 and 12 and §7 criterion 1 assert byte identity of whole prompts and do not.
suggestion: Name the mechanism per input rather than one mechanism for four: temp state directory for the round number, the consecutive-clean count and the output_path; an explicit workflow override (a task-file workflow block, or the TP_* environment the test sets) for the loop budget. Then have the test assert the resolved values it depends on before asserting on bytes, so a policy change fails with a legible message instead of a byte diff.

finding: §6.1's baseline construction — 'the test calls the prompt builder twice, once with the append enabled and once without' — buys a production-code toggle whose only false caller is a test. The append is unconditional in production (§1: 'The clauses are emitted on every path'; §2.3: appended to every prompt with a non-empty `output_path`), so an 'append enabled' parameter is a knob no shipped path ever sets, added to the one function this release touches. The baseline is obtainable without it: emit once, and the pre-clause body is the emitted body minus §2.3's fixed suffix — which is the same operation test 3 already performs.
suggestion: Restate §6.1's construction as 'emit once and strip the §2.3 suffix' rather than 'call the builder twice', or leave the acquisition mechanism to the task's acceptance and state only the requirement (an exact delta from the same tree, no tag, no stored blob). Either way, do not require a parameter that production never varies.

finding: Test 10 splits the refused modes by 'where the mode's own arguments can be omitted' versus 'where the mode cannot parse without them (--record, --resolve, --resolve-all take a positional)', and claims the first class 'makes it discriminating: it fails if the flag conflict is checked after argument validation'. Measured on the freshly built binary, the partition does not survive: tp review <spec> --status and tp review <spec> --report both exit 0 with no further arguments, so they land in the first class by test 10's rule while having no argument validation for the precedence rule to precede — those cases cannot fail for the reason test 10 gives. tp review <spec> --resolve-all exits 2 with its own usage error, i.e. it does parse and produce a competing message, contradicting its placement in the second class. The modes where §4.2.1's precedence rule is actually observable are --verify (exit 2, error '--verify requires --findings', which is the very hint §4.2.1 uses as its motivating example) and --merge (exit 2, 'looks like a spec') for review, and --merge for audit — and test 10 names none of them.
suggestion: Name the discriminating modes outright instead of deriving them from a property the spec does not let a reader evaluate: for --verify and --merge under tp review, and --merge under tp audit, assert that the hint names the --role conflict and NOT the mode's own missing argument; for every other refused mode assert exit 2 with a hint naming --role. That keeps the derived-not-enumerated spirit of test 4 while pinning the one case §4.2.1's precedence sentence exists for.

finding: Test 9 prescribes a single invocation shape — 'tp review <spec> --role <name>' — for all five skip reasons, but §4.2's own table qualifies one of them in the cell itself: 'no-spec-change (under --diff-from)'. That reason cannot arise from the invocation test 9 names, so that sub-case is unrunnable exactly as written, and an implementer either silently adds --diff-from (making the test something the spec did not ask for) or writes a case that cannot reach its precondition. The no-baseline sub-case has the same shape more weakly: it is reachable only at round 1, which test 7 states explicitly and test 9 does not, so the two tests describe the same case with different preconditions.
suggestion: Give test 9 the invocation per reason rather than one shape for five: no-spec-change under 'tp review <spec> --diff-from <ref> --role <name>'; no-baseline at round 1, or drop it from test 9 and cross-reference test 7 which already pins it; domain-mismatch, disabled-by-spec and no-checklist-items in the default mode. Then the sentence 'the test builds a fixture per reason' names what each fixture has to contain.

finding: Test 14 says 'for each unit BuildNextUnits returns, execute its brief_command and assert exit 0'. brief_command is a shell string beginning with the bare word tp (§4.2.2 fixes it as 'tp review <spec> --role <id>'), and §6.4 pins nothing about how it is executed: how the string is tokenised, which binary the name tp resolves to, or the working directory it runs in. That is load-bearing rather than pedantic here — this repository's PATH tp is deliberately a lagging release, and a test that shells out gets its verdict from an unstated environment. Three harnesses are equally consistent with the sentence (exec the string through sh, split on whitespace and exec, re-dispatch the parsed arguments through the cobra root in-process) and they do not have the same failure modes.
suggestion: Pin the harness in test 14: parse brief_command and re-dispatch its arguments through the in-process cobra root, so no PATH resolution or shell quoting is involved and the test cannot pass or fail on which binary is installed. Keep the string-shape assertion where it already is, in test 13, and say that test 13 pins the text while test 14 pins the behaviour.

finding: Tests 13 and 14 both require running the tp CLI and neither says which binary. Test 14 says "For each unit `BuildNextUnits` returns, execute its `brief_command` and assert exit 0", and test 13 asserts "end-to-end through `tp run --dry-run`". `brief_command` is the literal string `tp review <spec> --role <id>`, so executing it resolves `tp` on PATH — which in this repository is documented to be a lagging release that will not even recognise `--role`, making the test assert exit 0 against the wrong tree (or fail for an unrelated reason). §6.1 established the rule for the emitter ("a `go test` binary compiles one source tree — the current one"); §6.4 needs the same rule and does not state it. Test 13's `tp run --dry-run` half has a second unstated precondition: `tp run` reads `runner` from config and the fixture must supply one, which §6.4 never mentions.
suggestion: State the harness: build the current tree once with `go build -o <tmp>/tp ./cmd/tp` in TestMain (or use `go test`'s package binary via `os.Executable` + a subcommand shim) and execute `brief_command` with that path substituted for the leading `tp` token, asserting the substitution is the only edit. Name the `runner` value the test 13 fixture sets for `tp run --dry-run`.

finding: Criterion 2 asserts that the union of the per-role invocations' prompts[] equals the unrestricted prompts[] 'as an ordered sequence', and the phrase is doing the work of making the criterion strict. It cannot fail. The per-role invocations can only be enumerated from the unrestricted payload's own roles, so concatenating each single-entry result in that enumeration order reproduces the unrestricted order by construction. There is no implementation of --role that satisfies the equality half — every enumerated role returns its own entry — and then fails the ordering half. The ordering clause reads as the discriminating part of the gate's central criterion and adds no discriminating power over plain set equality.
suggestion: Either drop 'as an ordered sequence' and state set equality plainly, so the criterion does not claim strictness it lacks, or make ordering observable independently: invoke the per-role commands in sorted role-name order, and separately assert the unrestricted payload's role sequence against a pinned expected sequence for that spec and phase. The second form catches a reordered panel, which is what the phrase currently implies it catches.

finding: Gate criterion 3 mislabels the appended suffix as 467 bytes, and an implementer who builds the assertion literally gets an off-by-one in the opposite direction from the one round 4 fixed. Criterion 3 says "The v0.36.0 body equals the pre-clause body with its trailing newline removed plus §2.3's 467-byte suffix". The suffix §2.3 appends is `LF LF` + clause + `LF LF` + clause; measured on the spec's own literals, that is 2 + 287 + 2 + 177 = 468 bytes. 467 is the NET delta after the -1 strip, which criterion 3's own sentence has already accounted for separately by saying "with its trailing newline removed". So the criterion as written asserts body == strip(body) + 468 bytes while calling the second operand 467, and any expected-value the implementer constructs from that sentence is one byte short. §1's table is internally correct (-1 + 2 + 287 + 2 + 177 = 467) and §6.2 test 5's 467 is correct because it names a length DIFFERENCE, not a suffix — §7 is the only place the two quantities are conflated.
suggestion: Rewrite criterion 3 as "the pre-clause body with its trailing newline removed, plus §2.3's 468-byte suffix — a net delta of +467, the figure §1 tabulates and §6.2 test 5 asserts", so the suffix length and the net delta are never the same number in the same sentence.

finding: The gate is scoped 'per spec that has a role corpus' and closes with 'A spec with no role corpus is named as out of scope rather than silently skipped', but neither the predicate nor its evaluation is defined, so the gate's own scope is not testable. In this repository the corpus is repository-level (.tp/reviewers/ and .tp/auditors/), so on the plain reading no spec lacks one and the exclusion clause is empty; the only per-spec variation is role deactivation, which removes some roles rather than the corpus. It is also unstated whether the predicate is evaluated per phase while the gate is required to run 'for tp review AND tp audit' — a spec whose frontmatter deactivates every audit role would have a review corpus and no audit one, and the spec does not say whether that is in scope, half in scope, or a named exclusion.
suggestion: Define the predicate operationally and per phase, in terms the gate's own commands produce: 'a spec is in scope for a phase when the unrestricted invocation for that phase emits at least one prompt; otherwise the spec is listed by name, with the phase, in the gate's output as out of scope.' That makes both the scope and the naming requirement observable from the gate run itself, and removes the need for a separate notion of having a corpus.

finding: §7 gives a scope predicate and a count that select different sets, so the implementer cannot tell which specs the gate iterates. The predicate is "per spec that has a role corpus" and "A spec with no role corpus is named as out of scope"; the price is "on this repository's 15 specs". Measured: `spec/*.md` is 39 files, and `spec/.tp-review/*/` is exactly 15 — so 15 is the count of specs with recorded REVIEW STATE, not of specs with a role corpus. And the predicate itself is not computable as written: this repo has one repo-level corpus (`.tp/reviewers/`, `.tp/auditors/`) that `ResolveActiveCorpus` returns for every spec, so "has a role corpus" is true for all 39 unless it is redefined as "per-spec activation leaves the set non-empty", which §7 does not say. The gate is release-blocking, so the difference between 15 and 39 is a 2.6x cost error and, more importantly, an undefined iteration set. §7 also says the check runs "against the current tree only", which makes recorded review state irrelevant and so makes 15 the wrong basis on the spec's own terms.
suggestion: State the iteration set as a computable expression — e.g. "every `spec/*.md` for which `ResolveActiveCorpus` returns a non-empty set for the phase under test" — and re-derive the emission count from it (39 specs x 2 commands x roles-per-spec), or restrict the gate to a named list of specs and say why that list is sufficient.

finding: §7's cost paragraph counts emissions and prices them as 'seconds of CPU, no network and no agent', which is false for exactly the repositories this gate targets. Each of the ~150 emissions runs every registered `workflow.checks` command (review.go:540-543) — on this repository those are scripts, not arithmetic — and each rewrites that spec's `spec/.tp-review/<base>/snapshot-round-N.md` (§2.2's own observed side effect). So a release gate that exists because snapshots drift (§7 measures 35 of 145 rounds already drifted) itself rewrites the snapshot of every spec in the repository, and the price quoted omits both the check executions and the writes.
suggestion: Price the gate in the units it actually spends: ~150 emissions x (1 workflow.checks run + 1 snapshot rewrite), and state the write side effect explicitly. If the gate is to be non-mutating — which is what 'it is a test, not a cycle' implies — run it under the same fixed temporary state directory §6.1 already requires for the unit tests, and say so.

finding: The document states a rule about deferral and then breaks it in the same document. §3.1 concludes, after checking two candidate owners and finding neither: 'Naming a file that does not contain the question is worse than naming none -- it converts an open problem into a closed-looking reference.' Non-Goal 6 then does exactly that for the regression-unit question: '`spec/0.38.0.md` is the backlog release and so the natural home, but it does not contain the section today'. The hedge is honest, but it is the same move §3.1 ruled against, and Non-Goal 5 -- written for the sibling open question -- takes the opposite line ('No spec owns the question yet and §3.1 declines to name one'). Two adjacent non-goals apply opposite policies to the same kind of gap.
suggestion: Make Non-Goal 6 match Non-Goal 5: state the question and that no spec owns it, without naming a natural home. Or, if the rule in §3.1 is meant to permit a hedged pointer, say so there so both non-goals can follow it.
